Frequentar a escola em ﬁns de semana pode parecer uma ideia pouco atrativa para muitos estudantes.
No entanto, iniciativas que abrem os portões das instituições para a comunidade vêm transformando essa
percepção. No lugar de aulas, lições e provas, alunos, familiares e moradores do entorno encontram uma
programação voltada à cultura, ao esporte e ao lazer.
Nesse contexto, a comunidade deixa de ser vista só como destinatária das ações escolares ou local e ori-
gem dos alunos e passa a ocupar o espaço de parceira na construção de conhecimento, explica Luciana
Szymanski, coordenadora do grupo de pesquisa Práticas Educativas e Atenção Psicoeducacional na Escola,
Família e Comunidade (Ecofam), ligado à Faculdade de Ciências Humanas e da Saúde da PUC-SP.
Para ela, escolas que buscam conhecer o território onde estão inseridas e dialogar com famílias e equipa-
mentos culturais, esportivos e sociais da região tendem a dar mais sentido ao aprendizado. “O bairro é um
currículo vivo, é a vida acontecendo. Quando a escola se abre e se oferece para o território – sua história,
suas memórias, seus saberes, suas tensões, suas lideranças –, ela amplia imensamente o repertório educa-
tivo”.
Segundo Luciana, pesquisas mostram que escolas abertas nos ﬁns de semana sofrem menos agressões e
depredações. Ela aponta ainda que os efeitos positivos podem ser percebidos tanto em instituições públicas
quanto em privadas. “Vemos isso em áreas periféricas, mas também em zonas privilegiadas economica-
mente, onde escolas que incorporam a realidade local às práticas pedagógicas criam aprendizado muito mais
signiﬁcativo do que aquele que chega pronto nos livros didáticos”.
Esse ponto de vista é reforçado por Felipe Pregnolatto, coordenador do Midlle Years Programme do IB da
Beacon School. Ele aﬁrma que projetos como esses democratizam o acesso ao capital cultural e social e
jogam luz sobre vulnerabilidades estruturais. Na visão dele, para alunos em contextos mais vulneráveis, o
modelo oferece redes de apoio, mentorias e visibilidade, enquanto estudantes em contextos privilegiados são
levados a desenvolver a capacidade crítica de reconhecer os próprios privilégios e agir de forma ética para
ajudar na construção de uma sociedade mais justa.
Pregnolatto também aponta que iniciativas que aproximam a comunidade das escolas fazem parte do con-
ceito de território educativo, que transforma o bairro em uma extensão da sala de aula e propõe que o entorno
exerça um papel educador na vida dos alunos.
Os especialistas aﬁrmam ainda que a conexão entre a escola e a comunidade tende a ser uma estratégia
para lidar com problemas como a evasão. As instituições passam a atuar como rede de proteção ao oferecer
oportunidades que alunos, familiares e vizinhos não encontrariam em outros espaços. Para Pregnolatto, isso
ocorre porque o sentimento de pertencimento está ligado à segurança emocional e à motivação intrínseca.
“Quando um estudante percebe que sua identidade, sua história e sua comunidade são valorizadas e inte-
gradas ao ambiente escolar, ele se sente validado. O acolhimento reduz a evasão, mitiga conﬂitos e cria um
clima de cooperação que potencializa o foco e o sucesso acadêmico”, conclui.
(Adaptado de: HORA, Geovanna. Projetos que abrem os portões das escolas à comunidade beneﬁciam alunos e famílias. O Estado de
S. Paulo. São Paulo, 25 de jun. 2026. D4, .EDU.)

Acerca dos recursos linguístico-argumentativos empregados no texto, considere as aﬁrmativas a seguir.

THE INVISIBLE PRICE OF TRAVELLING SAFELY AS A WOMAN
At 23:00 on a wet Friday night in central London, I’m standing in the lobby of a pod hotel staring at two
nearly identical booking options. A capsule on a mixed-gender ﬂoor costs £35 ($47) whilst a capsule on the
women-only ﬂoor is £45 ($60).
The extra £10 doesn’t buy a better room. The capsules are exactly the same: compact cocoons ﬁtted with
a mattress, mood lighting and just enough space to fully open a small suitcase. What the surcharge offers
instead is a keycard-restricted corridor, a ﬂoor without men and, perhaps most importantly, the promise of
sleeping a little easier in an unfamiliar city.
Most of the women around me barely glance at the price difference. As I tap my card, I realize I’m not really
weighing one room against another. I am weighing whether my peace of mind is worth the extra £10.
Because of the risks of sexual harassment, and unwanted attention, travel often comes with a series of ﬁnancial
trade-offs for many women, such as paying more for centrally located hotels, taking taxis rather than walking
at night or choosing women-only spaces. It’s tempting to compare this with the “pink tax”, the term used to
describe products or services marketed to women at a higher price than equivalent versions for men. But the
costs of travelling safely are often less direct.
Women are not necessarily being charged more for the same journey. Instead, safety concerns push them
towards different – and sometimes more expensive – choices. Stephanie Boyle calls it an “avoidance tax”,
noting that women often alter their behaviour before anything has gone wrong. “Women aren’t travelling less
because they’re less adventurous than men,” she says. “They face a different risk environment.”
Research from the Safer Tourism Foundation, which tracks gendered travel behaviour, found that 64% of
women avoid walking back to their accommodation alone at night while abroad, compared to 43% of men, and
56% avoid areas they perceive as unsafe versus 37% of men. Nearly half of women (48%) avoid exploring
their destination at night altogether. These decisions also affect spending.
Solo female traveller Jen Kaarlo says solo travel for many women often comes with constant calculations
around safety. For Kaarlo, choices such as arriving in daylight, pre-booking transport and avoiding situations
where she feels overly vulnerable have become almost automatic. She frequently budgets extra for transport,
particularly when arriving somewhere unfamiliar. “Probably the biggest cost generally is the extra ground
transportation... I avoid mass transit anytime getting into a new city unless I know that city really well.” These
experiences have made her more conscious of the risks involved in travelling alone and more willing to pay for
peace of mind.
The reasons why women-only accommodation can be priced differently varies. A spokesperson for Generator
Hostels says the price of female-only dorms reﬂect demand rather than gender-based pricing.
The cost isn’t conﬁned to accommodation. Many women describe choosing convenience over spontaneity,

**THE INVISIBLE PRICE OF TRAVELLING SAFELY AS A WOMAN**

At 23:00 on a wet Friday night in central London, I’m standing in the lobby of a pod hotel staring at two nearly identical booking options. A capsule on a mixed-gender floor costs £35 ($47) whilst a capsule on the women-only floor is £45 ($60).
The extra £10 doesn’t buy a better room. The capsules are exactly the same: compact cocoons fitted with a mattress, mood lighting and just enough space to fully open a small suitcase. What the surcharge offers instead is a keycard-restricted corridor, a floor without men and, perhaps most importantly, the promise of sleeping a little easier in an unfamiliar city.
Most of the women around me barely glance at the price difference. As I tap my card, I realize I’m not really weighing one room against another. I am weighing whether my peace of mind is worth the extra £10. Because of the risks of sexual harassment, and unwanted attention, travel often comes with a series of financial trade-offs for many women, such as paying more for centrally located hotels, taking taxis rather than walking at night or choosing women-only spaces. It’s tempting to compare this with the “pink tax”, the term used to describe products or services marketed to women at a higher price than equivalent versions for men. But the costs of travelling safely are often less direct.
Women are not necessarily being charged more for the same journey. Instead, safety concerns push them towards different – and sometimes more expensive – choices. Stephanie Boyle calls it an “avoidance tax”, noting that women often alter their behaviour before anything has gone wrong. “Women aren’t travelling less because they’re less adventurous than men,” she says. “They face a different risk environment.” Research from the Safer Tourism Foundation, which tracks gendered travel behaviour, found that 64% of women avoid walking back to their accommodation alone at night while abroad, compared to 43% of men, and 56% avoid areas they perceive as unsafe versus 37% of men. Nearly half of women (48%) avoid exploring their destination at night altogether. These decisions also affect spending.
Solo female traveller Jen Kaarlo says solo travel for many women often comes with constant calculations around safety. For Kaarlo, choices such as arriving in daylight, pre-booking transport and avoiding situations where she feels overly vulnerable have become almost automatic. She frequently budgets extra for transport, particularly when arriving somewhere unfamiliar. “Probably the biggest cost generally is the extra ground transportation... I avoid mass transit anytime getting into a new city unless I know that city really well.” These experiences have made her more conscious of the risks involved in travelling alone and more willing to pay for peace of mind.
The reasons why women-only accommodation can be priced differently varies. A spokesperson for Generator Hostels says the price of female-only dorms reflect demand rather than gender-based pricing.
The cost isn’t confined to accommodation. Many women describe choosing convenience over spontaneity, picking options that feel safer. The question becomes not only “Can I afford this?” but “Can I afford not to?” And for Kaarlo, “The cognitive overload, I think, is the biggest weight,” she says.
Back in my London pod, I settle into my capsule and text my friends to let them know I’ve arrived safely after the night out. The extra £10 had bought the feeling of sleeping a little easier in a big city. But it leaves me with a more fundamental question: should feeling safe be something travellers have to pay extra for at all?

(Adaptado de: BOZKURT, Lorin. The invisible price of travelling safely as a woman. ~~BBC Travel~~, Londres, 10 ago. 2026. Disponível em: https://www.bbc.com/travel/article/20260807-the-controversial-economics-of-women-only-travel. Acesso em: 10 ago. 2026.)

b) O aumento de resgates em setores urbanos, como a construção civil, revela que formas extremas de exploração

c) A presença de migrantes e de populações pobres em atividades com vínculos frágeis de emprego amplia sua

e) A legislação que pune o trabalho análogo à escravidão atribui papel secundário às políticas públicas de proteção
